clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant vascular dysplasia caused by pathogenic variants in ACVRL1 (encoding ALK1), distinct from HHT1 which is caused by ENG (endoglin) variants.

Diagnosis rests on the Curacao criteria: recurrent spontaneous epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasia at characteristic sites, visceral arteriovenous malformations, and an affected first-degree relative.
Compared with HHT1, HHT2 tends to have a later onset of epistaxis and telangiectasia and a lower frequency of pulmonary and cerebral arteriovenous malformations.
Hepatic arteriovenous malformations are proportionally more common in HHT2 and can drive high-output cardiac failure, portal hypertension, or biliary ischaemia.
Mucocutaneous telangiectasia favour the lips, tongue, oral mucosa, fingertips and nasal mucosa, blanching with pressure.
ACVRL1 variants also underlie a recognised overlap with heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension, so unexplained dyspnoea warrants scrutiny.
Iron deficiency anaemia from chronic epistaxis and occult gastrointestinal telangiectasial bleeding is a major source of morbidity.
Screening for visceral arteriovenous malformations and genetic counselling of at-risk relatives are cornerstones of management.
reference.pathophysiology: HHT type 2 is an autosomal dominant disorder of vascular morphogenesis caused by loss-of-function variants in ACVRL1, which encodes activin receptor-like kinase 1 (ALK1), a type I receptor of the transforming growth factor-beta and bone morphogenetic protein superfamily expressed predominantly on endothelium. ALK1 signals with the co-receptor endoglin and downstream SMAD proteins to regulate the balance between endothelial quiescence and angiogenic activation; haploinsufficiency disrupts this signalling so that arterioles and venules develop with deficient intervening capillary beds, producing fragile direct arteriovenous communications. Small dilated post-capillary venules give rise to the characteristic mucocutaneous telangiectasia, while larger shunts form arteriovenous malformations in the lungs, liver, brain and gastrointestinal tract. The thin, poorly supported vessel walls bleed readily, and abnormal shunting alters regional and systemic haemodynamics, most notably the high hepatic arteriovenous flow that predisposes HHT2 patients to high-output cardiac states.
additionalDifferentials: CREST/limited systemic sclerosis with mucocutaneous telangiectasia
Von Willebrand disease and other bleeding diatheses causing recurrent epistaxis
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing for ACVRL1 variants with cascade testing of relatives
Contrast (bubble) transthoracic echocardiography to screen for pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
Contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging of the liver for hepatic arteriovenous malformations
Cerebral magnetic resonance imaging where cerebral vascular malformation screening is indicated
Full blood count and iron studies to quantify chronic blood loss
Faecal occult blood testing and endoscopy where gastrointestinal telangiectasia is suspected
redFlags: Progressive exertional dyspnoea, ascites or hepatomegaly suggesting high-output failure from hepatic arteriovenous malformations
Focal neurological deficit, seizure or severe headache raising concern for cerebral vascular malformation or paradoxical embolism
Haemoptysis or hypoxaemia indicating a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation
Haemodynamically significant epistaxis or gastrointestinal haemorrhage with symptomatic anaemia
reference.prognosis: With systematic screening for visceral arteriovenous malformations, iron replacement and targeted intervention many patients have a near-normal lifespan. Morbidity is driven chiefly by recurrent bleeding and, in HHT2 particularly, by complications of hepatic arteriovenous malformations.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent epistaxis to trivial causes and missing the familial vascular diagnosis
Assuming HHT2 carries the same pulmonary and cerebral arteriovenous malformation risk as HHT1 and under-appreciating hepatic involvement
Overlooking the ACVRL1 link to heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension in a breathless patient
Failing to caution against antiplatelet and anticoagulant exposure without weighing bleeding risk
Neglecting cascade genetic testing and screening of asymptomatic first-degree relatives
references: International guidelines on hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
management: Manage epistaxis in a stepwise fashion with nasal humidification and moisturisers, topical or oral tranexamic acid, ablative therapy such as laser or coagulation, and the antiangiogenic bevacizumab for refractory bleeding
Correct chronic bleeding-related anaemia with oral or intravenous iron replacement and transfusion when required
Screen for and treat pulmonary arteriovenous malformations by transcatheter embolisation to prevent paradoxical embolic stroke and cerebral abscess
Give antibiotic prophylaxis before dental and surgical procedures and observe air-embolism precautions in patients with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations

Manage the disproportionately common hepatic arteriovenous malformations and their complications of high-output cardiac failure, portal hypertension and biliary ischaemia, reserving liver transplantation for severe disease
Screen for associated pulmonary arterial hypertension when dyspnoea is unexplained
Genetic counselling, ACVRL1 testing and cascade screening of first-degree relatives
